6e22adf2296a.exp: The stern light (luz de alcance), white, covers an arc of 135º aft. The masthead light (luz de tope) covers 225º, the sidelights 112.5º each, and an all-round light 360º.

d524bbed3cb8.exp: Green over white all-round, with the green sidelight, is a trawler seen from its starboard side. A dredger would show red and green lights arranged differently, and a tug, yellow and white lights.

3eab2c710232.exp: Two white masthead lights, together with green and red sidelights, make up the tug seen head-on, with a tow of less than 200 m. A vessel constrained by her draught shows three red lights, and a power-driven vessel over 50 m shows two masthead lights but with the second one aft and higher, and no other signal.

dad55828177e.exp: Two cones joined at their apexes (hourglass) is the shape of a vessel engaged in fishing, which also shows it when at anchor or not making way. If the gear extends more than 150 m, she also carries a cone pointing up. They are not the shapes for a vessel at anchor (one ball) or constrained by draught (cylinder).

884a9e4d2f0f.exp: A black bicone shape, that is, two cones joined at their bases (diamond), indicates a tug whose tow exceeds 200 m (Rule 24 a ii). The fishing vessel shows two cones joined at their apexes, and the vessel constrained by draught, a cylinder. Mnemonic: diamond = long tow.

e547b03d1ff3.exp: The bicone shape (diamond) is shown by a tug with a tow of more than 200 m. A sailing vessel under power shows a cone with its apex down, the purse seiner shows a cone pointing up, and the vessel constrained by draught, a cylinder.

568895fa474c.exp: Red over green all-round at the masthead is the optional light of a sailing vessel, and the white stern light shows she is seen from astern. A fishing vessel would show red or green over white, and a vessel constrained by draught, three red lights in a vertical line. Mnemonic: red over green belongs to sail, which carries no masthead lights.

8e7bec2cfa73.exp: A white light over a red all-round light identifies a pilot vessel on duty; if she also shows one or two white anchor lights, she is at anchor. Under way she would show sidelights. A vessel aground shows two red lights in a vertical line and the anchor lights.

26d946484b70.exp: Red over white all-round is a fishing vessel other than a trawler. The white stern light that accompanies it shows we see her from astern, and the absence of visible sidelights is consistent with that: from astern only the stern light is seen. So she is seen from astern and making way, which is option d. If she were not making way she would not show sidelights or the stern light, depending on the case.

38661706bc90.exp: Red over white all-round, with green and red sidelights, is a fishing vessel other than a trawler seen head-on and making way. Mnemonic: trawling is green over white, all others red over white, and the sidelights show she is seen head-on. Constrained by draught would be three red lights.

410cd09abe8d.exp: The marks and lights of a spoil ground (vertedero) are yellow, the colour of IALA buoyage special marks, intended to mark areas for specific uses such as spoil grounds or anchorages. Red and green are not used because they indicate port and starboard.

e6dc77d9887f.exp: A power-driven vessel making way, in restricted visibility, sounds one prolonged blast at intervals of not more than 2 minutes (Rule 35 a). If stopped and not making way, she sounds two prolonged blasts. A sailing vessel sounds one prolonged and two short.

d992031739da.exp: According to Rule 8, whenever there is sufficient sea room, an alteration of course is the most effective action to avoid a collision, provided it is large and made in good time. A change of speed is less noticeable to the other vessel. Going astern or changing speed are second-choice resources.

06333257c53e.exp: A vessel engaged in fishing shows by day two cones joined at their apexes in a vertical line (Rule 26). If the gear extends more than 150 m, she adds a cone pointing up in the direction of the gear. Two cones with their bases together (diamond) are the shape for a long tow, and two balls mean not under command.

160af12c6c16.exp: A sailing vessel under power is a power-driven vessel and must show by day, forward, a black cone with its apex down (Rule 25 e). It is the shape that warns that, although she has sails, she must manoeuvre as a power-driven vessel. It is not the cone pointing up (fishing with long gear) nor the two opposed at their apexes (fishing).

801459f2b59b.exp: In poor visibility a safe speed must be maintained, appropriate to the circumstances and the visibility, and power-driven vessels must have their engines ready for immediate manoeuvre (Rules 6 and 19 b). It is not a fixed value, such as half the cruising speed.

985b72e7bec0.exp: A vessel at anchor of less than 50 m shows at least one white all-round light where it can best be seen (Rule 30). Only those under 7 m, outside channels and anchorage areas, are exempt. At 8 m, she must show it. Red lights are for a vessel aground or not under command.

d4b21b0fa03c.exp: A vessel at anchor of less than 50 m in length need only show one white all-round light in the forward part, where it is most visible. Red lights are not anchor lights (they indicate not under command, constrained by draught or aground), and the obligation to show a light exists at night, so it cannot be none.

1b6929306035.exp: When the vessel being towed is manned, in restricted visibility she sounds one prolonged blast followed by three short, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes, immediately after the tug's signal. It is the signal of vessels with restricted ability (long-short-short) extended by one more short blast: long + 3 short.

5ae0aee3a779.exp: A fishing vessel (not trawling) shows two all-round lights in a vertical line: the upper one red and the lower one white. These lights are added to the navigation lights if she is making way. Remember: red above, white below, 'red over white, fishing all right'. If trawling, the upper one is green over white.
5ae0aee3a779.duda: The key says 'green or red upper', but the rule distinguishes green (trawling) and red (others); the option is imprecise, and option c (red above and green below) is also incorrect.

327acb962b23.exp: With vessels in sight, one short blast means 'I am altering my course to starboard'; two short, 'I am altering my course to port'; three short, 'I am operating astern propulsion'. It also applies when leaving or entering a port when other vessels are in sight. Mnemonic: the number of blasts matches letters: one = S for starboard, two = P for port.

a27098896a0c.exp: Two red all-round lights in a vertical line identify a vessel not under command: she cannot manoeuvre as the COLREGs require because of an exceptional circumstance (breakdown). Do not confuse with the vessel constrained by her draught, which shows three red lights, nor with the vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre (red-white-red).

cb4de07c616c.exp: Five or more short, rapid blasts are the doubt signal: 'I do not understand your intentions' or 'I doubt that you are taking sufficient action to avoid collision'. It is sounded when vessels are in sight of one another and may be accompanied by light flashes. It does not indicate agreement or lack of control.

c4e939c25ce1.exp: Vessels of less than 20 m, like sailing vessels, must not impede the passage of vessels that can safely navigate only within a channel or narrow passage. It is a rule of not impeding, not a prohibition on overtaking: if overtaking is possible safely and with the proper signals, it may be done.

b7e2a26fe37e.exp: The stand-on vessel (the one with priority) must keep her course and speed so the other can predict her manoeuvre. Only if the give-way vessel does not act may she manoeuvre on her own, and always avoiding turning to port for a vessel that is on her port side. Changing course or speed unnecessarily creates confusion.

57dd1a4a3d17.exp: Vessels of less than 20 m in length, like sailing vessels, must not impede the passage of vessels that can safely navigate only within a narrow channel. It is about not hindering them, not a rule about the overtaking side or the sounding.

f6c3ba86ef4f.exp: To avoid a collision, the alteration of course must be large, clear and in good time, so that the other vessel notices it. A series of small successive alterations must be avoided because the other does not perceive them and may be confused. If there is sea room, it is even acceptable to pass astern of the other.

ea11748ab246.exp: A vessel is overtaking another when she approaches from a direction more than 22.5 degrees abaft the beam, that is, with a relative bearing greater than 112.5 degrees (90 + 22.5) on either side. In that sector the vessel being overtaken sees only the white stern light. If in doubt, assume you are overtaking.

0f8910342983.exp: The COLREGs establish (Rule 2) that nothing exonerates the vessel, the owner, the master or the crew from the consequences of any neglect to comply with the rules or of the neglect of any precaution which may be required by the ordinary practice of seamen. Complying only in part or sailing in poor visibility is no excuse; responsibility is not transferred.

9b0ebdaa2245.exp: Shapes (balls, cones, cylinders, diamonds) are the day signals equivalent to the night lights, and are shown by day. At night lights are used. In restricted visibility by day, shapes must also be shown and lights may be added as the rule requires.

3a558485a877.exp: In a narrow channel, a vessel wishing to overtake on the port side sounds two prolonged blasts followed by two short; on the starboard side, two prolonged followed by one short. The vessel being overtaken replies with the sequence long-short-long-short if she agrees. Mnemonic: the number of short blasts matches 1 = starboard (S) and 2 = port (P).

f0d58d35dad4.exp: Two red all-round lights in a vertical line indicate a vessel not under command. The green sidelight shows she is making way and is seen from her starboard side (green = starboard). Without way she would show only the two red lights. The vessel constrained by her draught shows three red, and the one restricted in her ability to manoeuvre red-white-red.

d3a6572403c3.exp: The key says she is not making way, but the drawing shows a green sidelight next to white lights.
d3a6572403c3.duda: The figure shows an upper white light, a green one and another white one below, that is, navigation lights; sidelights are shown only when making way, so it seems she would be making way and the key may be wrong.

8620adf384b8.exp: A power-driven vessel with a disabled engine, adrift and unable to manoeuvre as the COLREGs require, becomes a vessel not under command: the inability is due to an exceptional circumstance. A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre is so because of the nature of her work, not because of a breakdown.

29434fd94dc9.exp: Vessels of less than 12 m are not required to carry a whistle, bell and gong, but must carry some other means of making an efficient sound signal (for example, a hand whistle or a gas horn). So the equipment may be replaced, but the ability to signal may not be dispensed with.

6b23bf684853.exp: A sailing vessel must keep out of the way of a vessel engaged in fishing. In the COLREGs hierarchy: not under command, restricted in ability to manoeuvre, constrained by draught, fishing, sailing and lastly power-driven. Sailing vessels give way to all those before them, except for the exception of overtaking vessels.

e65ea2843445.exp: One prolonged blast at intervals of not more than 2 minutes in restricted visibility is the signal of a power-driven vessel under way and making way. If stopped and not making way she sounds two prolonged blasts. Fishing vessels, sailing vessels and vessels restricted in manoeuvre sound long-short-short.

e9b8556ec8c2.exp: Rule 6 requires proceeding at all times at a safe speed, one that allows effective action to avoid collision and to be stopped within a distance appropriate to the prevailing circumstances. Visibility, traffic and night are factors taken into account in setting it, but the obligation exists at all times.

1eacec015c34.exp: According to the COLREGs, a vessel is 'under way' (en navegación) when she is not at anchor, made fast to the shore, or aground. It does not matter whether the engine is running or the sails are hoisted: a drifting boat not under command is still under way. All three negative conditions must be met at once.

0d8edfae19e6.exp: 'Under way' (en navegación) is any vessel that is not at anchor, made fast to the shore, or aground. The other options include only one condition: not being aground is not enough, since she might be at anchor. Even with the engine stopped, as long as she is not in one of the three situations, she is considered under way.

5f2834b5df5a.exp: Two red all-round lights in a vertical line correspond to a vessel not under command and not making way. Even without way she is still 'under way' because she is not at anchor, made fast to the shore or aground. She would not be 'making way' (con arrancada), as she shows no sidelights or stern light.

16dd4910870c.exp: Vessels of 12 m to less than 100 m must carry a whistle and a bell. Those of 100 m or more must also carry a gong. Those under 12 m are not obliged to carry these devices, but must be able to make efficient signals by other means.

0b876079047d.exp: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, the one that has the other on her starboard side gives way; the other keeps her course and speed. According to the drawing, B is the vessel with priority, so she keeps her course and speed, and A must keep out of her way.

2a6ec63e9735.exp: With a northerly wind, A sails on 270 (west) and has the wind on her starboard side, while B sails on 90 (east) and has the wind on her port side. When sailing vessels have the wind on different sides, the one with the wind on the port side gives way, that is B. Mnemonic: 'port gives way, starboard stands on'.

04a262962c40.exp: Between two sailing vessels with the wind on different sides, the one with the wind on the port side keeps out of the way of the one with the wind on the starboard side. Here A has the wind on the starboard side and has priority, so B must manoeuvre. The head-on turn to starboard applies only to power-driven vessels.

1fce7f2f3e6a.exp: When two sailing vessels have the wind on different sides, the one with the wind on the port side must keep out of the other's way. So A gives way, as she has the wind on the port side. Being to windward or to leeward matters only when both have the wind on the same side.

2d9db988ccc4.exp: The COLREGs apply to all types of vessels, regardless of size or activity, on the high seas and in all waters connected to them navigable by seagoing vessels. They include sailing boats, pleasure craft, fishing vessels and merchant ships. The other options restrict their scope wrongly.

27d53f476091.exp: A is considered to be overtaking B when she approaches from a direction more than 22.5 degrees abaft B's beam. In that case B would see only A's white stern light. The overtaking vessel must keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken, whatever her type.

04d8d2f59776.exp: The drawing shows A approaching B from a sector more than 22.5 degrees abaft B's beam, that is with a relative bearing greater than 112.5 degrees. It is an overtaking situation, and the overtaking vessel must keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken.

acf4157a7e41.exp: A traffic separation scheme is crossed on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the general direction of the traffic flow, to minimise crossing time and confusion with the vessels using it. Crossing parallel or at small angles prolongs exposure.

20758d5e28e0.exp: The masthead light is white, placed over the fore-and-aft centreline, with an arc of 225 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on each side. The stern light, by contrast, covers 135 degrees aft. Together with the sidelights they cover the full 360 degrees on a power-driven vessel.

e11383ff03eb.exp: The stern light is white, placed as far aft as possible, and covers 135 degrees (67.5 on each side from right astern). It complements the 225-degree arc of the masthead light. The towing light is yellow and has the same 135-degree arc.

ceb9737801f0.exp: A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre is one that, by the nature of her work (laying cables, dredging, refuelling, operating submarines...), cannot keep out of the way as the COLREGs require. Do not confuse with not under command (due to a breakdown) or constrained by her draught (due to depth).

d66d6e5b5c8d.exp: The towing light is yellow, with the same characteristics as the stern light (135 degrees aft), and is placed above it. The tug shows it in addition to the towing masthead lights, and this distinguishes it from other power-driven vessels.

dc70fee9cfb5.exp: The masthead light is white, visible over an arc of 225 degrees forward. Green and red are sidelights (starboard and port), yellow is the towing light, and the all-round red is for a vessel not under command or restricted.

c963858f88ca.exp: The stern light of a sailing vessel is white, as on any other vessel, and covers 135 degrees aft. A sailing vessel under way shows sidelights and a stern light, and optionally a tricolour light at the masthead.

7b5c7559f77b.exp: The stern light is white and covers an arc of 135 degrees aft, 67.5 degrees on each side. Yellow is the towing light. Light colours: green starboard, red port, white ahead-astern, yellow towing.

fd2c352e73c9.exp: Two red all-round lights in a vertical line identify a vessel not under command; if she also shows sidelights and a stern light, she is making way. The vessel constrained by her draught shows three red and the one restricted in her ability to manoeuvre red-white-red. Aground: two red plus anchor light(s).

baba0d05010a.exp: A sailing vessel using engine and sail together is considered a power-driven vessel, and must show by day a black cone with its apex down. Pilot vessels, submarines or fishing vessels do not lose their status because of this. Mnemonic: if the engine is running, she is power-driven.

5886e8f35512.exp: Two black balls in a vertical line in the most visible position indicate a vessel not under command. A single ball indicates at anchor; ball-diamond-ball, restricted in ability to manoeuvre. Mnemonic: two balls = not under command, just like the two red lights at night.

f3b3e617d2b5.exp: The length of the tow is measured from the stern of the towing vessel to the after end of the last vessel or object being towed. If it exceeds 200 m, the tug shows a diamond by day and three white masthead lights at night.

7d70d2e11f42.exp: The COLREGs apply to all vessels on the high seas and in waters connected to it navigable by seagoing vessels, whether merchant, fishing or pleasure craft, with or without an engine. The rules distinguish hierarchies, but no class is left out.

a87b5e0ec608.exp: One prolonged blast followed by two short in restricted visibility is sounded by vessels not under command, restricted in their ability to manoeuvre, constrained by draught, sailing, fishing and towing. Among the options, only the sailing vessel. A power-driven vessel making way sounds one prolonged; not making way, two prolonged.

57761fe6d214.exp: If two sailing vessels have the wind on the same side, the one to windward (barlovento, where the wind comes from) keeps out of the way of the one to leeward (sotavento). Mnemonic: 'windward gives way', because she can manoeuvre more easily and the leeward vessel has her wind blanketed.

77bc67a5824c.exp: One prolonged blast every 2 minutes at most, in fog, is the signal of a power-driven vessel under way and making way. Not making way she sounds two prolonged, and the sailing vessel sounds long-short-short. The vessel at anchor uses a bell.

56babfb280dc.exp: Risk of collision exists when the bearing of the approaching vessel does not change appreciably. If the bearing stays the same, we are heading for the same point; if it changes, she will pass ahead or astern. In case of doubt, assume the risk exists. Mnemonic: constant bearing, danger.

ea23e834681c.exp: Long-short-long-short is the signal by which the overtaken vessel expresses her agreement to be overtaken in a narrow channel. It answers the overtaking request (two prolonged and one or two short). If in doubt, she would sound five short blasts.

741b78eba2e4.exp: Slowly and repeatedly raising and lowering outstretched arms is one of the distress and help-request signals in Annex IV of the COLREGs. Others are SOS by any means, flares, or the flag with a square and a ball.

88a8f6ea529c.exp: In a head-on situation between power-driven vessels, each alters course to starboard to pass port side to port side. It is one of the few rules where both vessels manoeuvre. Opposite or nearly opposite courses are recognised because both sidelights and the masthead light are seen.

4787d6dae2db.exp: Between a sailing boat and a power boat, in any situation (head-on or crossing), the power vessel keeps out of the way of the sailing vessel, unless the sailing vessel is overtaking. The rule of both altering to starboard applies only to two power-driven vessels.

117469257a53.exp: When a vessel overtakes another, she must keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken, whatever her type. A sailing vessel overtaking a power vessel does not have priority for being under sail: the overtaking rule prevails over the rule on vessel types. Mnemonic: 'whoever overtakes, gives way'.

42ce9bfc3efa.exp: With vessels in sight, one short blast means 'I am altering my course to starboard'. In restricted visibility the short blast has no such use; moreover, 'two short' indicates altering to port and 'three short' going astern. These are manoeuvring signals, not general warning signals.

bd5ebd20e3ea.exp: In overtaking, the overtaking vessel must keep out of the way, whether sailing or power. The general rule that power gives way to sail does not apply when the sailing vessel is the one overtaking: the sailing vessel keeps clear of the power vessel she is overtaking.

665c1de26499.exp: If the bearing of an approaching vessel changes appreciably, there is no risk of collision: she will pass ahead or astern. There is risk when the bearing remains constant. With very large or close vessels, risk may exist even when it changes, but the general rule is this one.

c010dd790de2.exp: A sailing vessel must keep out of the way of a vessel engaged in fishing, which according to the COLREGs hierarchy has priority over a sailing vessel. The drawing shows fishing lights, so we are the ones to manoeuvre. It does not matter that she approaches on our port side: the type of vessel weighs more than the side.

9c1f0b439f00.exp: In a crossing situation, the vessel that has the other on her starboard side gives way. The tug comes from our port side, that is, we are on her starboard side, so she must keep clear. The tug is a power-driven vessel with a tow, not a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, unless her work limits her.

0ae94aa4bd21.exp: The tug comes from our starboard side, that is, she has us on her port side and we see her to starboard. In a crossing between power-driven vessels, the one who sees the other to starboard gives way: us. Mnemonic: 'what I see to starboard, I give way to'.

c6d9d5621f63.exp: According to the drawing, the other boat crosses us from starboard to port, that is, we see her on our starboard side. In a crossing between power-driven vessels the one who sees the other on her starboard side gives way, which is us. That she is a fishing vessel changes nothing for a power vessel, since both have priority by side.

5433c2bb64c4.exp: The lights in the drawing (white masthead, green sidelight and white stern light) are those of a power-driven vessel that we see on her starboard side, that is, she crosses from port to starboard ahead of us. As we have her on our port side, we have priority and must keep course and speed. If the bearing is constant: that vessel must manoeuvre.

0a7937ab4055.exp: The vessel crosses on our port side, so we have priority and must keep course and speed. However, if the other does not manoeuvre, Rule 17 allows us to act to avoid collision, and we must do so by altering to starboard, never to port for a vessel that is on our port side.

a26a117f7952.exp: Even though the other vessel must keep clear, if we see she is not manoeuvring and there is risk of collision we must act to avoid it (Rule 17): the stand-on vessel may manoeuvre on her own as soon as she realises the other is not complying, and is obliged to do so when collision cannot be avoided by the other's manoeuvre alone.

3e1a60bb3b22.exp: Red over green all-round lights, with sidelights, are those of a sailing vessel under way. A power-driven vessel must keep out of the way of a sailing vessel. In a head-on situation the rule of altering to starboard is between power vessels, so here we may alter to either side, taking care to manoeuvre clearly and in good time.

d16c09d23bb0.exp: In a head-on situation between two power-driven vessels, both must manoeuvre by altering to starboard. That is why both give way. If the other were a fishing vessel, she would have priority only in a crossing, not in a head-on situation between two power vessels.

a6bf983d1439.exp: The overtaking vessel must keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken, whatever the type of vessel and the side on which she receives the wind. We are overtaking, so it is up to us to manoeuvre. Mnemonic: 'whoever overtakes, gives way'.

0abd6a5a4778.exp: The shape in the drawing, a black cone with its apex down, indicates the vessel is sailing and motoring at the same time, and is therefore power-driven. A power-driven vessel must keep out of the way of a sailing vessel, so the other one manoeuvres, even though we have the wind on the port side.

1d4c6ecbbbab.exp: With the wind on opposite sides, the vessel with the wind on the port side keeps out of the way of the one with the wind on the starboard side. We have it on the port side, so we give way. Being to windward or leeward counts only when both have the wind on the same side.

b99eefe7d443.exp: Red over green all-round with sidelights indicates a sailing vessel. We have the wind on the starboard side and the other on the port side, so we have priority: we keep our course and keep watch. The one with the wind on the port side must keep clear. This question appears in several versions with the same answer.

cef2e8b58737.exp: When two sailing vessels have the wind on different sides, the one with the wind on the port side gives way. We have it on the starboard side, so we keep our course, while keeping watch. If the other does not manoeuvre, we may act under Rule 17.

45971958f92b.exp: With the wind on the starboard side we have priority over the sailing vessel that has it on the port side. We keep course and speed with extreme vigilance, and only if the other does not comply will we manoeuvre. We should not alter to port or starboard unnecessarily.

2f766a8ff7a5.exp: The other sailing vessel's mainsail is sheeted out to starboard, which indicates she has the wind on her port side (the sail goes out on the side opposite the wind). We have it on the starboard side, so, with winds on opposite sides, the one with the wind on the port side gives way: the other vessel.

6f3a7ce3725c.exp: We have the wind on the port side and, according to the drawing, the other vessel is a sailing vessel that has it on the starboard side. With different sides, the one with the wind on the port side gives way, that is, us. Mnemonic: 'port gives way'.

1823b1a1cbf0.exp: We have the wind on the starboard side and the other on the port side: opposite sides. The one with the wind on the port side must keep clear, that is, the other vessel. We have priority and keep course and speed. Windward is used only if both have the wind on the same side.

4317f62c552c.exp: Two red all-round lights in a vertical line, plus the red sidelight, are those of a vessel not under command and making way seen from her port side. Being unable to manoeuvre, she has priority over the sailing vessel, which must keep clear of her path.

037b4434aa2c.exp: A sailing vessel must keep out of the way of a vessel engaged in fishing, which has priority in the COLREGs hierarchy. The shape in the drawing (two cones joined at their apexes) corresponds to a fishing vessel. The diamond is for a long tow or restricted ability to manoeuvre (ball-diamond-ball).

701cc07a3708.exp: Trolling does not count as fishing for the purposes of the COLREGs, because its gear does not restrict manoeuvrability. Therefore, she has no priority over a sailing vessel; being a power vessel, she gives way to the sailing vessel. The side from which she approaches is irrelevant.

4987bfb3cf30.exp: In the COLREGs hierarchy the sailing vessel must keep out of the way of the vessel engaged in fishing (with nets, longlines or gear that restricts manoeuvrability). The side from which she comes is irrelevant. We are the ones who must manoeuvre.

82c2ef235668.exp: The shape in the drawing is a black cone with its apex down: a vessel sailing and motoring at the same time, considered power-driven. A power-driven vessel must keep out of the way of a sailing vessel, so the other one manoeuvres, even though she crosses us on our starboard side.

946e261faa69.exp: Two diamonds or cones joined at their bases on a tug (tow of more than 200 m) indicate that the vessel has restricted ability to manoeuvre because of the tow. Sailing vessels must keep out of the way of vessels restricted in their ability to manoeuvre, so we are the ones to manoeuvre.

56c16ca2976b.exp: In a narrow channel, a vessel wishing to overtake on the starboard side sounds two prolonged blasts followed by one short, and on the port side two prolonged followed by two short. Mnemonic: one short = starboard; two short = port. The overtaken vessel replies long-short-long-short if she agrees.

773501e9b1a0.exp: One prolonged followed by two short, in restricted visibility, is sounded by vessels not under command, restricted in ability to manoeuvre, constrained by draught, sailing, fishing and towing. Among the options only the sailing vessel fits. The motor-sailer with her engine running would sound one prolonged (she is power-driven).

862ca333c020.exp: According to the COLREGs, a prolonged blast is 4 to 6 seconds and a short blast about 1 second. These durations make it possible to tell apart the manoeuvring and restricted-visibility sound signals.

f35daffe0ed1.exp: A prolonged blast lasts 4 to 6 seconds; a short one, about 1 second. It is a literal definition from Rule 32 of the COLREGs, which is worth memorising in order to interpret sound signals.

bd4e44c66b96.exp: Safe speed (Rule 6) must be determined taking into account, among others, the state of visibility, traffic density, manoeuvrability, at night the presence of background light, the state of wind and sea, and draught in relation to the available depth. Here only option a lists the correct factors accurately.

cd2c6bd5e4be.exp: Two red all-round lights in a vertical line indicate a vessel not under command. If she carries a red sidelight, she is making way and is seen from her port side (red = port). Without way she would show only the two red lights.

8132c6cfb7a0.exp: A tug seen from astern shows the white stern light and, above it, the yellow towing light, plus the sidelights depending on the angle. Yellow over white is the characteristic feature: a vessel towing, seen from astern.

a661f0e5012d.exp: The lights in the drawing (white masthead and red sidelight) correspond to a power-driven vessel seen from her port side. Red indicates port. A fishing vessel would also show red-over-white all-round lights, and a pilot vessel white-over-red.

3bb7436c46c9.exp: The lights shown are the navigation lights of a power-driven vessel seen from her port side: white masthead light and red sidelight. A dredger would show red and green lights in a vertical line, and a tug, two masthead lights in a vertical line plus the yellow one.

ad0a980df9c5.exp: Three red all-round lights in a vertical line identify the vessel constrained by her draught (restringido por su calado), whose draught in relation to the depth greatly limits her ability to deviate. It is an optional display. They can be confused with the two red lights of the vessel not under command.

dea14e26f74a.exp: Two cones joined at the apex (hourglass) are the shape of a vessel engaged in fishing. Two cones joined at the base (diamond) are for a tow of more than 200 m, and the vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre shows ball-diamond-ball.

3974b3ebed00.exp: Two cones joined at the base form a diamond or bicone, the shape of a tug with a tow length of more than 200 m. Fishing vessels use two cones joined at the apex. Mnemonic: diamond = long tow.

edab0d23db56.exp: Two cones joined at the base form the diamond, the shape for a tow of more than 200 m. Fishing vessels use cones joined at the apex (hourglass). The vessel constrained by her draught shows a black cylinder.

394b6d908ddd.exp: The diamond (two cones joined at the base) is the shape for a tow longer than 200 m. The fishing vessel shows two cones joined at the apex, and the vessel constrained by draught, a cylinder.

6c6a198b431b.exp: Two cones joined at the base form a diamond, which indicates a tow of more than 200 m. Towing more than one vessel carries no different specific shape. The fishing vessel shows two cones joined at the apex, and the vessel constrained by draught a cylinder.

f5e6f131ddb3.exp: Rule 5 requires keeping at all times a proper look-out by sight and hearing, as well as by other appropriate means (radar, VHF), according to the circumstances. It is not limited to fog: it is permanent. This is how the situation and the risk of collision are fully appreciated.

e3f260c18a13.exp: At anchor in fog you are still a vessel that can be run into, so Rule 5 (look-out by sight and hearing at all times) still applies. Even if fog limits vision, you must keep looking and listening for the signals of other vessels. Radar helps but never replaces the look-out, and being at anchor does not exempt you from it.

345c7a290843.exp: Rule 5 of the COLREGs requires a look-out by sight and hearing at all times, also at anchor and in fog. At anchor you can be run into by someone under way, so you must see and hear any signal. Limiting yourself to hearing or to radar is insufficient, and there is no exemption for being well anchored.

e494abd0b17d.exp: According to the COLREGs (Rule 5), every vessel must at all times maintain a proper look-out by sight and hearing appropriate to the circumstances, as well as other available means such as radar or VHF. Neither the autopilot, nor the depth alarm, nor the radar, nor the VHF replaces the person keeping watch. Look-out is always mandatory, not only in fog.

0db8f76c3933.exp: According to the COLREGs (Rule 5), every vessel must at all times maintain a proper look-out by sight and hearing appropriate to the circumstances, as well as other available means such as radar or VHF. Neither the autopilot, nor the depth alarm, nor the radar, nor the VHF replaces the person keeping watch. Having the VHF switched on does not exempt you from keeping a look-out.

975e444f8a56.exp: The inshore traffic zone (zona de navegación costera), next to the traffic separation scheme, is in principle reserved for vessels of less than 20 m, sailing vessels and those that, by their service or authorisation, are entitled to use it. The key point for the exam is that only vessels that have authorisation to do so may use it; it is not limited only to fishing vessels or only to sailing vessels.

3c1fd8be21dc.exp: A sailing vessel under way shows only sidelights (green to starboard, red to port) and a white stern light; no masthead light visible from ahead, since she is not using mechanical propulsion. Seen head-on, both sidelights are seen. A fishing vessel adds all-round lights red over white or green over white, and the vessel constrained by draught shows three red.

f60596f5dbf9.exp: A vessel engaged in fishing shows two all-round lights in a vertical line: red above and white below (not trawling) or green above and white below (trawling), plus the sidelights if making way. It is the characteristic combination that distinguishes her; a vessel being towed does not carry those all-round lights and the vessel constrained by draught shows three red in a vertical line.

9e6334991dea.exp: A sailing vessel under sail alone shows only sidelights and a stern light, or a combined or tricolour light at the masthead. Seen head-on, the green and red are seen. Fishing, towed and constrained-by-draught vessels carry all-round lights or characteristic shapes that do not appear here.

9e29c9bb5fa9.exp: Flag A of the International Code of Signals means 'I have a diver down; keep well clear at slow speed'. A vessel engaged in diving operations that, because of her size, cannot show the three required lights or shapes must hoist a rigid replica of that flag, at least one metre high, visible all round the horizon.

d5335c533ef1.exp: The COLREGs manoeuvring signals are: one short, I am altering my course to starboard; two short, I am altering my course to port; three short, my engines are going astern. Mnemonic: the number of short blasts matches 1 starboard, 2 port, 3 astern. The prolonged blast is an attention signal or a warning at bends and when leaving a berth.

08f9808caee7.exp: A tug seen head-on shows two white masthead lights in a vertical line (three if the tow exceeds 200 m), sidelights and, aft, the yellow towing light above the stern light. A fishing vessel carries all-round lights red/white or green/white, one not under command two red, and a pilot vessel white over red.

ec51f95a8bef.exp: Vessels of less than 20 m and sailing vessels must not impede the safe passage of power-driven vessels following a traffic lane. Therefore, if possible, they should use the adjacent inshore traffic zone. Crossing must be done on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles, not at 45º, and one does not navigate in the separation zone.

d7165cb04ad1.exp: A dredger with an obstruction shows two red lights in a vertical line on the side where the obstruction is (do not pass) and two green on the side on which you can pass. We must pass on the clear side, the one with the green lights, so, according to the drawing, we alter towards it, which here turns out to be port. Red = danger, green = clear passage.

ce85a64f9ab3.exp: A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre by dredging shows two black balls in a vertical line on the side of the obstruction (do not pass) and two cones with apexes joined (diamonds) on the side on which you can pass. According to the drawing, the clear passage is to starboard, so we must alter to starboard. Balls = blocked, diamonds = pass.

18c2a1e4d8f7.exp: A tug whose tow length exceeds 200 m shows as a shape a bicone (two cones joined at their bases) in the most visible position. It is the day shape corresponding to that case; the balls and the combination of three shapes belong to other situations, such as the vessel restricted by dredging.

95d462d94b64.exp: Rule 30 of the COLREGs exempts vessels aground of less than 12 m in length from showing the aground lights and shapes (two red and one white, or three balls). So an 11.5 m yacht aground is under no obligation to hoist any shape. From 12 m she should hoist three black balls.

d31648ffb262.exp: The towing light is yellow, with the same characteristics as the stern light, that is, with a 135º arc of visibility aft, and is placed above it. It is neither white nor all-round. Mnemonic: the stern light is white, the towing light is yellow, both 135º.

80692f53ef7e.exp: The towing light is yellow and covers a 135º arc, like the white stern light above which it is placed. Its purpose is to tell whoever approaches from astern that the vessel has a tow. It is neither all-round nor white.

fd298b37987c.exp: Vessels at anchor of 50 m or more show a white all-round light forward and another, lower, aft. If they are 100 m or more, they must also illuminate their decks with working lights or equivalent. So for a 120 m length this full combination applies.

5b600da3b030.exp: A vessel at anchor of less than 50 m in length may show a single white all-round light in the most visible position, instead of the two lights of larger vessels. Red lights in a vertical line indicate not under command or constrained by draught, not anchoring. Only the vessel under 7 m, outside channels or anchorage areas, is exempt.

df305845ccdf.exp: Vessels at anchor of 50 m or more show a white all-round light forward and another, lower, aft. If they are 100 m or more, they must also illuminate their decks with working lights or equivalent. So for a 120 m length this full combination applies.

07392552e7d4.exp: A vessel at anchor of less than 50 m (15 m here) must show at least one white all-round light in the most visible position. Only vessels of less than 7 m, outside channels, anchorages or traffic areas, are exempt. Red lights do not belong to anchoring.

4f5cc07e7a46.exp: When manoeuvring, the COLREGs signals are: one short blast, I am altering my course to starboard; two short blasts, I am altering my course to port; three short blasts, I am going astern. Two short therefore indicate the vessel is altering to port. Rule: the number of short blasts is 1 starboard, 2 port, 3 astern.

c1629492ab70.exp: The COLREGs manoeuvring signals are: one short, I am altering my course to starboard; two short, I am altering my course to port; three short, I am going astern. Two short blasts therefore mean the vessel is altering to port. Mnemonic: 1 starboard, 2 port, 3 astern.

d70b1e36bd20.exp: Two red all-round lights in a vertical line identify the vessel not under command (NUC): one that, through an exceptional circumstance, cannot manoeuvre as the COLREGs require. If she is making way she adds sidelights and a stern light. Not to be confused with the one restricted in her ability to manoeuvre (red-white-red) or the one constrained by draught (three red).

0040e9779fd5.exp: A continuous sounding with any fog-signalling apparatus is the signal of distress and need of assistance, like red rockets, SOS, flag NC or orange smoke. It does not correspond to anchoring or grounding, which have their own specific bell and gong signals. It is used when there is serious danger.

0c405b1dec5a.exp: Three black balls in a vertical line are the day shape of a vessel aground, equivalent to the anchor lights (white all-round, or one forward and one aft) plus two red all-round lights in a vertical line. A single ball indicates at anchor; the vessel not under command shows two balls.

532338986ccf.exp: Three black balls in a vertical line are the shape for a vessel aground. The vessel at anchor shows a single ball forward, the one not under command two balls, and the one restricted in her ability to manoeuvre ball, diamond, ball. Three balls = three points on the bottom.

3c9797e73778.exp: A single black ball hoisted in the forward part is the shape for a vessel at anchor. The vessel aground shows three balls, the one not under command two, and the pilot vessel does not use this shape. Remember: one ball = anchor; three balls = touched bottom.

61a6cf2a5868.exp: Among the distress signals of Annex IV of the COLREGs is dense orange-coloured smoke. It indicates danger and need of assistance, along with red rockets, flares, SOS, flag N over C or a continuous sound. It is not a storm warning signal or one for other activities.

38b2d4844eaa.exp: Three balls in a vertical line indicate the vessel is aground. The vessel not under command shows two balls and the fishing vessel a double cone (bicone) or two cones joined at the apex. Here the shape is that for aground, since the drawing shows three balls.

7413d1ea20cb.exp: Flag A of the International Code of Signals means 'I have a diver down; keep clear at slow speed'. It therefore indicates a vessel engaged in diving operations. Neither anchoring nor grounding nor restricted draught is signalled with this flag.

f31f4a4f3719.exp: The shape of three black balls in a vertical line identifies the vessel aground. The vessel not under command shows two balls, the fishing vessel cones joined at the apex, and the one constrained by draught a cylinder. Mnemonic: three balls = aground, one = at anchor.

bd81bcec9c91.exp: According to Rule 9, sailing vessels and vessels of less than 20 m must not impede the passage of vessels that can safely navigate only within a narrow passage or channel. There is no absolute prohibition on overtaking them nor is a specific side set: the essential thing is not to impede.

abe6b5d78432.exp: According to Rule 9, sailing vessels and vessels of less than 20 m must not impede the passage of vessels that can safely navigate only within a narrow passage or channel. There is no absolute prohibition on overtaking them nor is a specific side set: the essential thing is not to impede.

e3f00d655a8a.exp: Rule 6 lists the factors for safe speed: state of visibility, traffic density, manoeuvrability, at night the background light from shore lights or backscatter, state of wind, sea and currents, and draught in relation to depth. With radar, other factors are added, but the option that gathers the general factors is the correct one.

d932053e0ff3.exp: Rule 8 requires manoeuvres to avoid collision to be large, clear and made in good time, avoiding a succession of small alterations of course and/or speed, which the other vessel would not notice. Altering to starboard or passing astern is not discouraged in itself; what must be avoided are the small successive alterations.

a137de590924.exp: In a narrow channel, the vessel that wants to overtake another on her starboard side sounds two prolonged blasts followed by one short. If on the port side, two prolonged followed by two short. The vessel being overtaken expresses agreement with one prolonged, one short, one prolonged, one short.

0d7bfb6a5db4.exp: In a narrow passage or channel, the vessel intending to overtake another on her starboard side sounds two prolonged blasts followed by one short. On the port side it would be two prolonged and two short. Agreement is indicated with long-short-long-short.

1efb457505c8.exp: The COLREGs light rules apply in all weather conditions from sunset to sunrise, and in restricted visibility also by day. They are not prohibited by day nor exclusive to the night: hence the correct option speaks of all conditions from sunset to sunrise.

8849da3906bc.exp: An overtaking vessel is one that approaches another from a direction more than 22.5º abaft the beam, that is, with a relative bearing greater than 112.5º, so that she could see only her stern light. 90º plus 22.5º is 112.5º. With the stern light (135º, 67.5º on each side) the overtaken vessel notices the situation.

3659f550e571.exp: The vessel that approaches another from a direction more than 22.5º abaft the beam of the latter is overtaking. In terms of bearing this equals more than 112.5º, but here it is expressed relative to the beam, so the answer is 22.5º. It corresponds to the sector of the stern light.

c90cdcbdd1e8.exp: If we leave the sailing vessel on our port side, we are overtaking her on her starboard side, and in a narrow channel the signal for that is two prolonged blasts followed by one short. To overtake on the port side it would be two prolonged and two short. The typical confusion is mixing up the side of the vessel overtaken with one's own.

1a3bba951bff.exp: A square flag with a ball above or below it is one of the distress signals of Annex IV of the COLREGs and means danger and need of assistance. It is not a regatta signal or a storm warning.

c814f6353f27.exp: In restricted visibility, the pilot vessel on duty sounds, in addition to the signals for her status (one prolonged, two prolonged...), an identity signal of four short blasts. Two prolonged indicate under way but stopped and not making way; therefore two prolonged followed by four short corresponds to the pilot vessel stopped and not making way.

8b4cdbc41423.exp: A ringing of the bell for about five seconds is the signal for at anchor. Pilot vessels on duty add the identity signal of four short blasts. Therefore, bell ringing plus four short indicates a pilot vessel at anchor.

09c5edb6ce1c.exp: A vessel at anchor, in restricted visibility, rings the bell for about five seconds at intervals not exceeding one minute (and vessels of more than 100 m also a gong aft). A single prolonged ringing, without blasts, indicates a vessel at anchor.

8fe743bdb5d3.exp: One prolonged followed by two short is the restricted-visibility signal of a sailing vessel, fishing vessel, vessel not under command, restricted in ability to manoeuvre, constrained by draught or tug, under way. Among the options, the only one that fits is the sailing vessel. A power vessel making way sounds one prolonged, and not making way, two prolonged.

c36b327bac09.exp: A vessel making way must show sidelights. If she shows only a masthead or stern light (or an all-round white), it indicates she is not making way, as when at anchor or stopped. Sidelights are what reveal that the vessel is moving through the water.

e3effc6626a1.exp: A vessel sailing and motoring at the same time is considered power-driven and must show by day forward, in the most visible position, a conical shape with its apex down. Remember it as 'one cone down = motor and sail together'. Balls, baskets or bicones have other meanings.

5520b1bdcf2c.exp: A ringing of the bell for about five seconds is the signal for at anchor, and the four short blasts are the identity signal of the pilot vessel on duty. Combined, they indicate a pilot vessel at anchor. A fishing vessel at anchor would make the at-anchor signal, with no special blasts.

e1e81ecf02b3.exp: According to the COLREGs definition, a vessel not under command is one that, through some exceptional circumstance, is unable to manoeuvre as required by the Rules, as happens after an engine or steering failure. Restricted ability to manoeuvre is due to the nature of the work, not to a breakdown, and the lack of an engine does not make her anchored.

af3c4bcac485.exp: A vessel not under command is one that, through an exceptional circumstance such as an engine failure, is unable to manoeuvre as required by the COLREGs. Restricted ability to manoeuvre is due to the nature of her work, not to a breakdown. She shows two red all-round lights or two balls.

e81ea2b60660.exp: A vessel not under command is one that, through an exceptional circumstance such as an engine failure, is unable to manoeuvre as required by the COLREGs. Restricted ability to manoeuvre is due to the nature of her work, not to a breakdown. She shows two red all-round lights or two balls.

d0d32eb6ff80.exp: A fishing vessel with gear extending more than 150 m horizontally shows a conical shape with its apex up in the direction of the gear. That is, the cone with its apex up marks the side on which she has the gear out; avoid passing on that side. The cone pointing down, on the other hand, indicates sail and motor at once.

b6e64c83abfa.exp: A fishing vessel with gear extending more than 150 m horizontally shows a conical shape with its apex up in the direction of the gear. That is, the cone with its apex up marks the side on which she has the gear out; avoid passing on that side. The cone pointing down, on the other hand, indicates sail and motor at once.

55a159d18dc8.exp: A fishing vessel with gear extending more than 150 m horizontally shows a conical shape with its apex up in the direction of the gear. That is, the cone with its apex up marks the side on which she has the gear out; avoid passing on that side. The cone pointing down, on the other hand, indicates sail and motor at once.

59759083141a.exp: A vessel aground of less than 50 m shows a white all-round light, that is, a 360º arc of visibility, plus two red all-round lights in a vertical line. All anchor and aground lights are all-round; they do not have 112.5º, 135º or 225º sectors.

9a599bd511cd.exp: The cone with its apex up indicates the side on which the fishing vessel (or other vessel with gear) has gear out for more than 150 m. We therefore must not pass on that side. It does not refer to towing nor to sail and motor, which uses a cone with its apex down.

ae3343bda054.exp: Rule 13 of the COLREGs establishes that any vessel overtaking another must keep out of her way, whatever her type. Although a sailing vessel normally has priority over a power-driven vessel, here the overtaking vessel, the power-driven one, is the one that must manoeuvre.

5f0e052bb168.exp: According to Rule 25, a sailing vessel of less than 7 m that cannot show the sidelights and stern light must have ready at hand an electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light. She must show it in sufficient time to prevent collision. She does not need all-round green or red lights.

751b7cc81f57.exp: A white all-round light with sidelights is the combination permitted for power-driven vessels of less than 12 m, in place of the masthead and stern lights. A vessel over 50 m carries two masthead lights, and the fishing and pilot vessels show red and white or green all-round lights.

b3edea0767a6.exp: In a narrow channel, two prolonged blasts followed by one short mean the vessel intends to overtake another on her starboard side. On the port side, two prolonged and two short are sounded. Long-short-long-short is the agreement of the vessel being overtaken.

52b3c8f827dc.exp: In restricted visibility, one prolonged blast every two minutes is a power-driven vessel making way, and two prolonged blasts with an interval of about two seconds indicate a power-driven vessel under way but stopped and not making way. The signals of fishing vessels, pilots and others are one prolonged and two short, or with four short.

ac75542dc5c1.exp: A vessel at anchor with the shapes in the drawing (ball, or balls and diamonds if working as a dredger) cannot keep out of the way; we must leave her on the side indicated by the shapes. According to the drawing, that side is port. If she were an ordinary anchored vessel, one could pass freely on either side.

9de3e244a03a.exp: A tug seen from astern shows the yellow towing light above the white stern light, both of 135º, and the masthead lights are not seen from behind. The vessel constrained by draught shows three red lights in a vertical line, which do not appear in this case. So it is the tug seen from astern.

74e7cbfc3a7a.exp: According to Rule 18, a sailing vessel must keep out of the way of a vessel engaged in fishing, because the fishing vessel has priority. The order of priority is: not under command, restricted in ability to manoeuvre, constrained by draught, fishing, sailing and finally power-driven. So B must manoeuvre.

4743b71868a2.exp: With a left-handed (counter-clockwise) propeller going astern and without way, the paddle-wheel effect (efecto de paleta) pushes the stern to port (the opposite of a right-handed propeller, which would take it to starboard). With the rudder amidships there is no rudder effect to compensate.

fd90f122cca4.exp: A wind from astern pushes the boat forward, so the lines that hold her back must be reinforced: the stern line (largo de popa), which works aft, and the bow spring (esprín de proa), which runs from the bow aft. A wind from ahead is countered with the bow line (largo de proa) and the stern spring (esprín de popa).

7a7b5b0b0c56.exp: To ease (lascar) is to let go or slacken a little a line that is under load, that is, to give more slack or pay it out slightly. Pulling in a line is hauling in (cobrar), gathering it in coils is coiling (adujar), and securing it with a knot is making fast (hacer firme) or mooring.

28c64d360622.exp: The stern spring (esprín de popa) runs from the stern forward and prevents a boat moored alongside from moving aft. The bow spring, on the other hand, prevents her moving forward, while the head and stern lines and breast lines fix the distance to the quay.

67eaa4be0555.exp: To raft up (abarloar) is to moor a boat alongside another, normally with fenders between them. To anchor (fondear) is to hold with an anchor, to turn around (ciabogar) is to turn in a small space, and to fend off (defenderse) is to protect oneself from knocks. Pass from the sides to rafting up to the quay.

8f62f4e9c3f0.exp: A wind from ahead pushes the boat aft, so the lines that prevent that movement must be reinforced: the bow line (largo de proa), which works forward, and the stern spring (esprín de popa), which runs from the stern forward. With a wind from astern, the stern line and the bow spring are reinforced.

00f87dc4656d.exp: To turn around (ciabogar) is to turn the boat in the smallest possible space, normally with one propeller ahead and the other astern, or with the rudder to one side and one engine astern. It is not making a 360º turn nor putting the bow into the wind. It is a pivot-turn manoeuvre.

55accb50bff2.exp: Set (deriva) is the displacement that the current causes in the vessel's track. Leeway (abatimiento) is that caused by the wind. From both and the vessel's speed the course made good is obtained. Terms such as distanciamiento or derrotamiento do not exist.

4006d04b42e2.exp: With a wind from ahead, the stern spring (runs from the stern forward) is kept and the rest are let go. Going slow ahead, the spring acts as a pivot point and the bow opens away from the quay, with the rudder to the quay side to help. The bow breast line and the bow line fix the bow and do not open it.

154f85354926.exp: Way (arrancada) is the residual speed a vessel keeps when propulsion ceases. If she has way she keeps moving through the water, so it must be taken into account when braking, berthing or anchoring. Steerage way is the minimum for the rudder to be effective.

67610ada4a66.exp: The port propeller ahead pushes the port side forward and the starboard one astern pulls the starboard side aft, so the boat turns to starboard and the bow falls off to starboard. Rule: the bow goes toward the side of the propeller that is going astern.

adbbd5f56623.exp: To make fast (hacer firme) is to secure a line with an easily released knot (for example, turns and a half hitch) so that it stays fixed. To take up the tension (templar) is to give it just the right tension, to ease (lascar) is to let go a little and to haul in (cobrar) is to gather by pulling.

66224764b31c.exp: To take up the tension on a line (templar) is to give it just the right tension, neither slack nor about to break. To ease (lascar) is to let go a little, to coil (adujar) is to gather it in a coil and to heat (calentar) is to haul in vigorously or to over-tension.

725bf9ee7e80.exp: The eye (gaza) is the loop formed at the end of a line, which is put over a bollard. The turn (vuelta) is the wrapping of the line around an object, the bight (seno) is the curved middle part and the knot is the actual tie.

3e455a1cea79.exp: The bow line (largo de proa) runs from the bow forward and prevents a boat moored alongside from moving aft. The bow spring, on the other hand, prevents her moving ahead, and the breast line fixes the side perpendicular to the quay. The stern-to line (codera) is a stern line in bows-or-stern-to mooring.

6875cb78ae87.exp: To pick up a buoy, approach with the bow into the wind (or the current) for better control. If the wind is NW, the bow must point NW, that is, on course 315º. Remember that the wind is named by where it comes from, and the course is where the bow is going.

e65d9d615557.exp: Set (deriva) is the deviation of the vessel from her course by the effect of a current. Not to be confused with leeway (abatimiento), which is caused by the wind, nor with magnetic variation nor with the length of the arc of parallel (departure, apartamiento).

748a43f48d58.exp: In bows-or-stern-to mooring (amarre de punta, stern to the quay), the lines running from the stern diagonally to the quay, crossed, are called stern lines (codera). They serve to hold the stern to the quay and prevent it swinging. The head line and the spring belong to alongside mooring.

97f8c13a4d3b.exp: With a wind from ahead the boat tends to go aft, so the lines that hold her in that direction must be reinforced: the bow line and the stern spring. The coderas, stern breast lines and the bow spring correspond to other cases.

401a4749bc8c.exp: With way ahead, for the bow to fall off to port the wheel is put to port, so the blade turns to port and pushes the stern to starboard. The wheel and the blade move in the same direction as the bow's turn when going ahead.

6ee198cb4936.exp: To heave (virar) is to haul in a line, cable or the anchor chain with a winch, capstan or windlass. To pay out (arriar) is to slacken or lower, and to take turns or belay (tomar vueltas o afirmar) is to secure a line so it does not move.

2d09a4221976.exp: To pick up a buoy, approach with the bow into the current (or the wind if it dominates), because that way the boat advances slowly over the bottom and steers better, and can stop without being pushed against the buoy. With the current from astern or the quarter, control would be lost.

0d9c20df1a96.exp: Bollards (norays) are the iron posts on the quay where the mooring lines are made fast. Eyes (gazas) are the loops of the lines, props (puntales) are supports and moorings blocks (muertos) are concrete weights anchored on the bottom.

eb0c6a9351a5.exp: Approach the buoy with the bow into the wind. If the wind comes from the NE, the bow must point NE, that is, on course 045º. Remember that the wind is named by where it comes from, and the course is where the bow is going.

231ac3ebbf90.exp: The vessel's turning circle (curva de evolución) has three phases: manoeuvring phase (start of the turn with the rudder), variable phase (the turning radius keeps changing) and uniform phase (steady circle). It does not include the swinging of the stern as a phase.

7e92c65c3813.exp: Going astern, the rudder acts the opposite way: if we want the bow to fall off to starboard the stern must go to port, so the rudder must be put to port. In addition, the propeller effect acts on this side.

e4c1ef2f3c52.exp: With the starboard propeller ahead and the port one astern, the couple makes the boat turn to port, that is, the bow falls off to port. It is the typical manoeuvre for turning around (ciabogar): the bow goes toward the side of the propeller that is going astern.

8fbefd7deea6.exp: The eye (gaza) is passed from below upward through the eyes of the other lines, so that any line can be let go without having to remove the others. That way each boat can slip her own line without freeing those of others.

7055f2e91b91.exp: To haul in (cobrar) is to pull a line taut and gather it in. To belay and to make fast (afirmar, hacer firme) is to secure it, and to take turns is to put turns around a fixed point to jam it.

50c30b917c92.exp: To cast off (largar) is to unmoor a line and leave it free. To haul in (cobrar) is to gather it, to coil (adujar) is to gather it in a coil and to lash (trincar) is to secure it firmly.

2571c9924560.exp: The stern line (codera) is the line led from the stern (or the bow) to a buoy, a mooring block or the opposite quay, to keep the boat away from the quay so she does not knock against it. It is confused with fenders, but these only cushion the rubbing; the codera is a mooring line.

b4fc918abd0a.exp: To haul in a line (cobrar) is to pull it and gather it aboard. It is the opposite of to pay out or ease off (filar or arriar, letting go). To make fast is to secure it by taking turns on a bitt or cleat; to take up tension (templar) is to give it just the right tension.

35886ebe4043.exp: To coil (adujar) is to gather a line by winding it in orderly turns (a coil, aduja) so it is ready for use without tangling. Putting an eye on a bollard is to bend or moor (abozar or amarrar); to slacken gradually is to ease or pay out (lascar or filar).
